title: Three levels of command
summary: From the gentle て-form request through なさい to the blunt command form, plus the two meanings of な.

blocks.text: Japanese has several ways to tell someone to do something. Think of them as a ladder from soft to hard.

rows: 待って, 泣かないで
parent to child, teacher to class

blocks.text: A bare **て-form** is a shortened "... please": 待って is 待ってください with the ください dropped. A request to *stay in a state* uses いる: **待っていて** (shortened 待ってて) means "stay waiting", with the feeling that it will not be for long. To forbid, use the special て-form **ないで**, short for ないでください.

blocks.en: Stay waiting here. (just for a moment)

blocks.text: **なさい** goes on the い-stem and is a firm but legitimate order from someone with the right to give it. A short form **な** on the い-stem means the same thing.
Do not mix it up with the **negative な**, which goes on the whole clause (the dictionary form), and means "don't".

The 命令形 uses the え-stem of a godan verb (行く → 行け) and ろ for an ichidan verb (食べる → 食べろ). Irregular: する → しろ, 来る → 来い, くれる → くれ. It is rough: friends, anger, sports, emergencies, or someone who really has the authority.

items: The softest is the **て-form**; **なさい** is a parent's order; the **command form** is the hardest.
A な on the い-stem means "do"; a な after the whole verb means "don't".
のだ (宿題をするのだ) and ように can also work as commands.
